item.title: At least 13 killed in Ukrainian drone strike deep into Russia
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgjvgv926po?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
At least 13 killed in Ukrainian drone strike deep into Russia - Published At least 13 people have been killed in a Ukrainian drone strike on the Russian republic of Tatarstan, officials have said. One child was among the victims with 75 more people injured, Russian authorities said, in one of the deadliest single attacks on Russia since the start of Moscow's full-scale war in Ukraine. Drones struck Nizhnekamsk, more than 1,100 kilometres (680m) from the Ukrainian border. Ukraine's Armed Forces confirmed Nizhnekamsk's Tanevo oil refinery had been hit, while Ukrainian defence technology manufacturer FirePoint said its FP-1 drones had been used in the attack. The strike lasted several hours overnight and into the morning, local sources say. Oil refineries in Nizhnekamsk had already been hit on 12 June. Verified images on social media show large plumes of smoke and flames rising into the sky in daytime, with air raid sirens howling in the background. Kyiv has recently stepped up its strikes on facilities it says contribute revenue and logistics to Russia's war on Ukraine. "The facilities Ukraine targets are used to carry out attacks against Ukraine, manufacture weapons, support Russia's war effort," said Andriy Kovalenko, head of the Ukraine's Centre for Countering Disinformation. Moscow confirmed industrial facilities were targeted but added residential areas were struck, too. "Civilian individuals who were not involved in any military operations were present," Russia's Investigative Committee said. The BBC has not independently verified this information. The head of Tatarstan, Rustam Minnikhanov, confirmed the strike and shared his condolences with the families of the deceased. "This is a tremendous pain for all of us," said Nizhnekamsk mayor Radmir Belayev. A period of mourning has been declared in Tatarstan. Ukraine's Kovalenko said "every civilian death in Russia is on [President Vladimir] Putin" and that "Russians should direct their grievances at Putin and at the decisions made within their own country". "Without Putin, there would have been no aggression. Without the aggression, these people would still be alive." More than 450 Ukrainian drones were also shot down by the Russian air defences overnight, Moscow said. Kyiv has become increasingly successful at carrying out long-range strikes on Russia, often targeting warehouses or energy infrastructure, with civilian casualties mounting. Russia, meanwhile, continues to target Ukraine with regular large-scale aerial attacks on cities and residential centres. Last week, a combined drone and missile strike on Kyiv killed 21 people. And in Kharkiv, near the front line, five people were killed overnight in a Russian artillery attack.

item.title: Evidence that South African special forces murdered top detective shared with BBC
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly8djwgem0o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Evidence that South African special forces murdered top detective shared with BBC - Published Senior police detective Frans Mathipa had been fighting for four months to gain access to a crucial piece of information in the case he was working on. Finally, he was told, it was going to come his way. But he feared his pursuit of it could cost him his life. Two days later, his car was found overturned - he had been shot dead while driving. Now seven members of South Africa's special forces, and one military police officer, have been charged with murdering Lt Col Mathipa, a highly respected officer, in August 2023. They deny the charges. There has been no date scheduled for their trial, and there are concerns it will never go ahead, because three of the men charged with his murder have refused to comply with a court order revoking their bail. They are still working for the army's special forces, and one of them has been promoted. The BBC World Service has been given exclusive access to the prosecution case against all the men. The case has caused consternation in one of Africa's most robust democracies, with fears the country's military is significantly overreaching its mandate. We asked the South African army whether it was responsible for Mathipa's killing. It did not respond. Several hundred pages of secret police and court documents, shared with the BBC, set out the evidence suggesting special forces killed Mathipa - who worked for an elite police unit known as "The Hawks". We have also interviewed key sources in the police investigation - South Africa's former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks; Mathipa's commanding officer; and Mathipa's family - to build the most comprehensive public account of the events leading up to the detective's death. It presents a compelling case that South Africa's special forces are responsible for his murder. In particular, police documents show that the vehicle that trailed Mathipa just before he was shot was registered to a front company for the special forces. And that tracking data found in that vehicle puts it at the scene of the shooting. One of the men in the car, Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, the documents show, was also spotted at the scene of an alleged abduction carried out by special forces soldiers - the case that Mathipa had been investigating. After Mathipa's death, special forces issued a chilling warning to The Hawks, the police documents say. "You can appoint 10 investigating officers; we will kill all of them," said the warning, according to police. South Africa: Anatomy of a cover-up Africa Eye uncovers a disturbing story of power, secrecy and murder. Watch on iPlayer - or listen on BBC Sounds to the podcast, Special forces on trial Episode two of the film available from 24 August. The case Mathipa had been investigating was sensitive. It centred on an Ethiopian man called Abdella Abadigga, an alleged so-called Islamic State [IS] militant. He had been granted temporary asylum in South Africa in 2008, but was arrested abroad in 2017. Abadigga had then been smuggled back into the country, by the South African military and Department of Home Affairs, to be used as an intelligence asset - but had "gone rogue", according to Col Tollie Vreugdenburg, former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks. Abadigga had gone on to extort Johannesburg's Ethiopian neighbourhood, sources in the community told us. This money was used to fund IS, says the US government. We asked the South African army if it had facilitated Abadigga's return to South Africa. And we asked the Department of Home Affairs if it had lied about a planned deportation of him to Ethiopia, and had instead smuggled him back into South Africa on an expired passport and refugee permit. They did not respond. Specifically, Mathipa was investigating the allegation that special forces had then gone on to abduct and kill Abadigga in December 2022 - who the United States, earlier that year, had put under sanctions, designating him an IS recruiter and fundraiser, as well as a trusted supporter of Bilal al-Sudani, a top IS figure in Somalia. Court documents show that after Abadigga's abduction, his phone connected to a mast near a military base. Police sources say it was used to call a number in Somalia. The Pentagon did not respond to the BBC's question on whether Abadigga's phone helped locate al-Sudani, who was killed by US special forces in Somalia in January 2023, only a few weeks after Abadigga's alleged abduction. We also asked South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa whether Abadigga had been kidnapped at the behest of the US. He declined to comment. When Mathipa was assigned the case, four months before his own death, he already knew special forces were implicated, but he was trying to secure more evidence. He was building on information already gathered by Abadigga's brother, Ameen - who had opened a missing person's case soon after the disappearance, and had been assigned an investigating officer (IO) from local police. He and the IO had obtained CCTV footage showing the last known movements of Abadigga and his bodyguard Kadir Abotese at the Mall of Africa, a shopping centre on the outskirts of Johannesburg. The footage, clips of which the BBC has seen, shows a man in a blue top following Abadigga and his bodyguard as they leave the food court to head back to the car park, and paying for parking three seconds after Abadigga and Abotese do. The mall CCTV footage contains another vital clue. The licence plates of the suspected kidnappers' vehicles are clearly visible. The vehicles were all registered to a company called Peters Communications Trust (PCT), a front company for South African special forces - Ameen and the IO were to discover. At the time of Abadigga's disappearance, PCT's directors included Maj Gen Herbert Mashego, the then commanding officer of 5 Special Forces Regiment. Police documents say a meeting was arranged between the IO and high ranks of the military, including Brig Gen Yalo, the then head of special forces, at which the IO was instructed to tell Ameen there was no link between PCT and the military. So, with the investigation seemingly at a standstill, Abadigga's brother took his case to the Johannesburg High Court. Responding to Ameen's legal action, special forces denied all knowledge of Abadigga or his whereabouts. They did, however, admit their soldiers had been at the Mall of Africa on the date in question, but said they had been there for a training exercise. They named the man seen wearing blue on CCTV as Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, and said he had been the exercise commander. They also admitted all the suspect vehicles seen at the mall belonged to them. Domestic operations by South Africa's military need to be authorised by both the government and the presidency. We asked South African former Defence Minister Thandi Modise, and President Ramaphosa, if they had authorised a training exercise in the Mall of Africa - Modise did not respond and Ramaphosa declined to comment. When Mathipa was assigned to the case a month later, he issued a subpoena to special forces to force them to hand over full details of this alleged training exercise and all the personnel involved. When access to these documents was finally promised, three months later, Mathipa had a premonition that he would be murdered - according to Brig Paulina Sekgobela, his commanding officer. "When [Mathipa] left my office he said: 'Brigadier, you know, these people - they are going to kill me. I'm going to die'," she told the BBC. On the day Mathipa was killed, he was phoned by a man calling himself Tebogo, who claimed he had information on the case for the detective - according to Mathipa's daughter Basetsana, who was home with him at the time. Mathipa and Tebogo arranged to meet at a petrol station in Pretoria. When Tebogo failed to show, Mathipa drove away again, along the highway. He was killed while driving, by rounds fired from high-velocity weapons which special forces would have had access to, according to South African police. And footage from motorway toll gantries, police say, shows one of the occupants of the black BMW, which tailed Mathipa moments before his murder, was Maj Sunnybooi Wambi. This car, like the three vehicles connected with Abadigga's disappearance at the mall, was registered to PCT, they add. New detectives were assigned to the case after Mathipa's death, triggering a chilling message from special forces, that made its way to the police's Criminal Intelligence division. Police say it warned that, however many investigating officers were assigned to the case, "we will kill all of them". Twelve members of the South African military have been arrested in total, including Lt Col Sunnybooi Wambi, and the current head of South Africa's special forces, Brig Gen Solomon Lechoenyo - both promoted to these positions since police first started investigating their roles in the case. The 12 have been variously charged with the abduction and murder of Abadigga and Abotese, the murder of Mathipa, fraud, and obstruction. All deny all charges and they were initially released on bail. But six of them later had their bail revoked, and were ordered to turn themselves in to custody. Three of the six, including Wambi, have been charged with both Mathipa's murder, and Abotese's abduction and murder. The military has refused to hand them over. In July, their lawyers cited mental health treatment for their absence. Three years after Mathipa's killing, no trial date has been set. Meanwhile, Abadigga's body has never been found. "[Mathipa] was barking up the right tree. He was taking on the right lion," Vreugdenburg says of the late detective. Mathipa's daughter Basetsana puts it starkly: "We need justice. I'm never going to see my dad anymore... Why my dad? Because he was doing his job."

item.title: China evacuates one million from homes as massive storm arrives
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2rgzyplg2o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
China evacuates one million from homes as massive storm arrives - Published Chinese authorities have evacuated more than a million people from their homes in eastern China including the financial capital Shanghai, as Typhoon Dolphin made landfall. The typhoon brought heavy rain and halted transportation across the region. Nearly 1,000 flights were cancelled in Shanghai alone on Monday. While authorities have downgraded Dolphin to a tropical storm, they continue to warn of torrential rains, severe flooding and the risk of landslides through to Wednesday as the storm moves north. Chinese authorities had earlier issued their highest-level red alert for Dolphin, which is the strongest storm to hit China this year. It packed maximum wind speeds of 150km/h (94mph) when it first slammed into Yuhuan in the Zhejiang province at 17:30 (09:30 GMT) on Sunday before making a second landfall in the city of Wenzhou about an hour later, meteorological authorities said. Heavy rain was forecast on Monday for the provinces of Shandong, Henan, Hubei, Anhui, Jiangsu, Zhejiang and the city of Shanghai. Governments have urged people to avoid outdoor activities, while several top tourist attractions remain closed, including parts of Disneyland and Legoland, and several viewing platforms along the Bund in Shanghai. Footage on state media show ground-floor businesses flooded in the former French Concession in Shanghai, an area popular with tourists, and people wading through ankle-deep waters. Several state media outlets have reported that a nine-year-old boy from Wenling, Zhejiang is missing after being swept into the sea. Chinese officials have not reported any casualties. Parts of Zhejiang could receive 250mm to 500mm of rain over the next few days, forecasters say. Authorities in Hangzhou, Zhejiang's capital city, have waived parking fees in all public spaces for drivers seeking shelter amid the strong winds and floodwaters. Elsewhere in the province, Wenzhou authorities have relocated some 900,000 residents and opened more than 1,000 emergency shelters, while about 390,000 people have been evacuated from their homes in the city of Taizhou. In the coastal province of Fujian, maritime authorities have suspended dozens of passenger ferry routes and halted more than 100 offshore construction projects. The storm moved over a long distance of 6,000km before making landfall, suggesting a lifespan of more than three times that of an average typhoon, according to China's state broadcaster CCTV. It also has a massive circulation size and intense rainfall capacity, CCTV reported. Misinformation around the storm has apparently spread rapidly on the Chinese internet, with state media reporting that two people have been detained for distributing such content. One of them, a 60-year-old man, created a fake video with AI that claimed someone in Shanghai had fallen from a building during the storm. Another man, 32, had re-edited storm footage posted by other social media users in a way that was deemed as misleading. Dolphin brought torrential rains to the Philippines, parts of northern Taiwan and Japan's Okinawa island before bearing down on China. - AI or real? BBC analyses viral China disaster videos - Published4 days ago Eight people have died in the Philippines because of heavy monsoon rains brought on by Dolphin and storms earlier in the week, says the Office of Civil Defence. More than 7,000 people are sheltering at evacuation centres nationwide. In Okinawa in Japan, five elderly people suffered non-life-threatening injuries, according to the prefectural government. Three of them fell because of the strong winds, it said. Meanwhile in Hong Kong, weather observatory posted a record high temperature of 36.9C on Sunday as the typhoon swept warm air over the city. Typhoon season in the western Pacific typically occurs between May and October, when typhoons are considered more commonplace. This year is a strong El Niño year, which experts say means typhoons can grow to be more intense.

item.title: Former Thai MP allegedly kills official and confesses on YouTube
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqx7lje8l79o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Former Thai MP allegedly kills official and confesses on YouTube - Published A former Thai MP allegedly shot dead a local official in the southern province of Nonthaburi, then dialled into a YouTube livestream to inform the host - a political pundit - of what he had done. Former Nonthaburi MP Chalong Reawraeng told the shocked host, Anchalee Paireerak, that he had shot Thongchai Yenprasert, a former police official, outside Thongchai's office. Thongchai, who was hit in the neck, died in hospital. His driver was shot in the arm and hand. Chalong was arrested but then allowed to hold a press conference at a police station where he attempted to explain what had happened while smoking a cigarette. He told the reporters there that Thongchai was "angry" at him, but did not explain why. He also said he did not intend to shoot Thongchai, whom he described as a "good friend". Chalong said he told Thongchai that he wanted to talk to him. According to local media reports, the two were involved in a personal dispute. "He [Thongchai] then pushed me, saying 'I don't want to talk, I don't want to talk.'" Chalong said he then followed Thongchai towards his car. "When I pulled the gun out, I didn't intend to shoot him. But then [Thongchai's driver] pulled his gun out and pointed it at me, so I fired." Thongchai, a retired police colonel, was president of the Nonthaburi Provincial Administrative Organisation or PAO, a local government body. Earlier, Chalong had called political commentator Anchalee Paireerak, who was livestreaming on YouTube at the time, to confess to the incident. Anchalee was filmed picking up a call midway through her programme. "I'll call you back... Oh, something big [happened]? Go ahead, what's that?" she said. Viewers could not hear what the caller said next, but Anchalee was seen reacting in shock. "Did he die? Did he die? You shot him in the head? You need to wait there for the cops," she said on the video, which was seen by the BBC. "Don't go anywhere." Monday's shooting came three days after a 14-year-old boy shot dead eight people at his home and school, then killed himself, in Thailand's worst mass shooting since 2022. The two attacks are not related. The latest shooting will further spur debate about gun control in Thailand, which has the highest rate of gun ownership in South East Asia by a wide margin. After Friday's school shooting, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul ordered tougher enforcement of gun laws and said police would set up checkpoints as part of a crackdown. Other measures would include tightening controls on the possession, carrying and use of firearms.

item.title: Alleged rebel leader killed in Colombia as president targets armed groups
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5yrljp9x9eo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Alleged rebel leader killed in Colombia as president targets armed groups - Published A man suspected of leading a dissident faction of a left-wing rebel group has been killed in a military operation in central Colombia, officials say. The operation forms part of a crackdown on illegal armed groups ordered by Colombia's new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, who was sworn in on Friday. He said the killing by the security forces of Hernando Forero Mosquera and five other alleged members of armed groups on the weekend sent "a clear and powerful message to all bandits that there is nowhere for them to hide". During his campaign for the presidency, de la Espriella said he would target "narco-terrorism" relentlessly, including by launching air strikes. Military intelligence officers said that Forero led a group known as Frente 28, which is one of the many dissident factions to have sprung forth from the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc). The Farc, Colombia's largest left-wing rebel group, signed a peace deal with the government in 2016 but some of its members did not agree to the terms of the deal and refused to lay down their arms. These dissidents groups, which are now mainly involved in cocaine trafficking and illegal mining, are among the main driving forces behind the resurgence in violence in the country. De la Espriella said he would take a radically different approach to defeating criminal groups in the country than his predecessor in office, Gustavo Petro. Petro, the first left-wing politician to be elected president of Colombia, advocated what he called a "total peace" strategy, which prioritised negotiation over confrontation. His attempts to negotiate with a number of armed groups, however, failed as members of the illegal organisations repeatedly broke ceasefires and walked away from the talks. De la Espriella's combative approach has been met with defiance by dissident rebel groups. On Saturday, just a day after the was sworn into office, two explosive devices went off. In Cauca province, a car bomb exploded at a tollbooth, injuring two security guards, and in Cesar province, a police officer was killed by explosives dropped from a drone. In a video uploaded to social media, de la Espriella praised the military for killing Forero, who was also known as "El ruso" (The Russian), and whom he described as an explosives expert. He added that three more alleged members of the dissident group had been killed in the military operation in a rural area in Meta province. The president also said that soldiers had killed two alleged members of another criminal group, the Gulf Clan, in a separate offensive in Antioquia province. De la Espriella has the backing of US President Donald Trump, who endorsed his candidacy. On Friday, the US state department said it planned to provide $1bn (£740m) in security assistance to de la Espriella's government. It also welcomed Colombia into the US-led group dubbed "Shield of the Americas" - an alliance of Western Hemisphere countries which have pledged to co-operate in their fight against drug trafficking gangs and transnational crime.

item.title: World's oceans hit record-high July temperatures
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cpvw8vmmgrwo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
World's oceans hit record-high July temperatures - Published The world's oceans hit their hottest ever recorded temperatures for July, partly fuelled by developing El Niño conditions in the Pacific, according to the EU's climate monitoring service. The average sea surface temperature (SST) outside the world's polar regions - between 60 degrees north and 60 degrees south - was 20.96C last month, beating the previous high of 20.89C, set in 2023. Last month was the joint second-warmest July globally on record, with temperatures 1.47C above the estimated pre-industrial average, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service. Meanwhile, Western Europe experienced its hottest ever June and July, with prolonged hot and dry conditions fuelling extreme wildfires across the region. Elsewhere, the UK is braced for its fifth heatwave of the year this week, as persistent dry weather puts further pressure on water supplies and could see more areas officially declared in drought. - What is El Niño and why could it mean record temperatures? - Published11 June - Rhine falls to record low levels as drought strains Europe's rivers - Published6 days ago Around Europe, sea surface temperatures in July reached record highs along the Atlantic coast and in the western Mediterranean, contributing to widespread strong and severe marine heatwaves. Sea temperatures remained exceptionally high across much of the tropical Pacific, where El Niño conditions are developing and forecast to strengthen in the coming months. El Niño is a natural weather pattern in the Pacific that combined with human-driven global warming can cause temperature spikes and more extreme weather. Oceans are a vital regulator of the climate, absorbing most of the excess heat generated by greenhouse gas emissions and producing half of Earth's oxygen. The greatest effect of ocean warming is on sea level rise. As seawater warms it expands, and this thermal expansion accounts for roughly a third of sea level rise recorded by scientists to date. That water encroaches on low-lying coasts and island nations. Hotter seas are also driving longer and fiercer marine heatwaves, which have bleached coral reefs on a mass scale and decimated kelp forests and fisheries. Warmer ocean surfaces also evaporate more heat and moisture into the air, intensifying tropical storms and loading them with heavier rainfall. 'Climate change is intensifying heat extremes' Western Europe is experiencing an exceptional run of extreme heat - with record-breaking temperatures in June and July, and some areas facing their third or fourth heat wave since May. The average temperature across western Europe for June and July was 21.62C - 2.79C above average and the highest for the two-month period. "July 2026 was the third consecutive month of exceptional heat in western Europe," said Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts. Persistent high-pressure systems trapped heat over the region, she said, while dry soils reduced the ability to provide natural cooling. "This is a clear example of how climate change is intensifying heat extremes, with heat and drought increasingly reinforcing one another," she added. France, Spain, parts of Germany and the UK recorded exceptionally low rainfall and/or soil moisture, while soil moisture levels across much of western Europe were significantly lower than in 2022, when the region experienced severe drought. River levels have been much lower than average - in some places exceptionally low -with the Seine, Rhine and Danube among those particularly affected. Low flows exacerbate pressure on water supplies and irrigation, aquatic ecosystems, river transport and energy production. The prolonged hot and dry conditions have created favourable conditions for wildfires, with massive wildfires raging across western Europe last month and "exceptional activity" in terms of the area burned and smoke and emissions generated. "Climate change is increasingly bringing the kinds of hot and dry conditions that favour large, high-intensity wildfires in southern Europe while extended the fire season northwards," said Laurence Rouil, director of the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service. Larger fires produce more smoke and inject it higher into the atmosphere, allowing it to travel much further, he said. That means countries that experience relatively few wildfires could be increasingly affected by smoke traveling long distances. Extreme weather 'new normal' In the UK, meanwhile, the prolonged dry spell is increasing pressure on already-stretched water supplies. England and Wales recorded their driest July since records began 190 years ago, according to the Met Office, while large parts of England and all of Wales have already been officially declared in drought. The Environment Agency has warned that more areas of England could be declared in drought if dry conditions persist. Weather that was once considered extreme is becoming the "new normal", according to the latest Met Office report on the UK's climate. Its latest assessment found that the hottest day of the year in southern England is now 4.5C warmer than it was between 1961 and 1990. "We are right now living in a time of historic and unprecedented change," said Mike Kendon, Met Office climate information scientist, adding that "evidence shows the climate of the 20th century has now gone". Scientists say El Niño may temporarily push global temperatures even higher. Its effects are being felt against a backdrop of man-made warming, particularly the burning of fossil fuels. The world is now about 1.4C warmer on average than it was in the late 19th Century. Related topics - Published13 hours ago - Published15 July

item.title: India police fire tear gas at protesters seeking exam reforms
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c89nkz4vjyxo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
India police fire tear gas at protesters seeking exam reforms - Published Police in India have fired tear gas shells on protesters demanding reforms to recruitment exams in the eastern state of Jharkhand. Thousands of students, job seekers and volunteers have been trying to reach the state's assembly in the capital city of Ranchi to register their protest. The BBC has seen some people who have sustained injuries, though the official number of injured is unclear. The protesters have been demonstrating for over two weeks now, demanding an overhaul of Jharkhand's government exam system. On Monday, many attempted to breach police barricades, causing police to use water cannons, batons and tear gas to try and disperse crowds, officials say. Ranchi City Superintendent of Police Paras Rana told ANI news agency that most protesters had been peaceful, but accused a smaller group of breaking through barricades and throwing stones at officers. He said three policemen had been injured. "About 90% of the students are peaceful, but there are some who are not listening even to their own representatives," he said. Rana said police had shown restraint and used "minimal force for a very short time" because the protesters were students. He appealed to them to remain peaceful, saying their demands were reaching the government. The protest comes weeks after thousands of young Indians attempted to march to the national parliament in Delhi, amid the massive "cockroach" protests over exam paper leaks. India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - which is not a political party - called off its five-week-long protest on 25 July after education minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned. The CJP had attracted support from students based in different states of the country. Meanwhile in Ranchi, visuals from the state capital show thousands of protesters, police as well as media personnel on the streets, amid tightened security arrangements. Despite police efforts to disperse them, large crowds remain at the site. Protesters in Jharkhand have been gathered at a stadium in Ranchi since 25 July - some have been sleeping in the open and several have gone on hunger strike. Even after multiple rounds of talks and the government accepting several demands, protesters say the agitation will continue until all their demands are met. The immediate cause of the anger is a preliminary civil service exam held by the Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) in April. After the results were announced in July, candidates alleged that leaked answer sheets shared on social media showed some successful applicants had answered far fewer questions than expected. This fuelled suspicions that the results had been manipulated. The state government has assured students that they will get justice. The allegations around the exam are being investigated by Jharkhand's Criminal Investigation Department (CID). More than a dozen people have been arrested. Investigators are also examining the role of a private company that conducted parts of the exam process after candidates raised questions about how it was selected. After talks with protesters on Sunday, the government agreed to cancel the exam in question, along with two others. Three JPSC members also reportedly resigned. This came after JPSC chairman L Khiangte stepped down on 22 July. He was questioned in the investigation and arrested on Monday. But protesters say several demands remain unmet, chief among them an investigation into the irregularities by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), India's premier federal investigative agency. Unlike the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protests, which emerged outside party politics, the Ranchi agitation has drawn strong political backing. The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) , which is in opposition in Jharkhand, has backed the protesters, staged demonstrations, raised the issue in the state assembly and demanded a federal investigation. Congress, a partner in the state government but the BJP's national rival, has also expressed support for the students. On Sunday, Jharkhand Chief Minister Hemant Soren, who is the head of the regional Jharkhand Mukti Morcha (JMM) party, alleged that vested interests were trying to disrupt democracy in the state. He warned that the protesters' agitation should not be politicised and also reiterated his promise to take action to deliver justice.

item.title: 'Body in suitcase' found in Australia turns out to be lifelike doll
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyqg4w3gz9o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'Body in suitcase' found in Australia turns out to be lifelike doll - Published Australian police called in to investigate a body found in a suitcase have concluded that the "victim" was in fact a lifelike doll. The suitcase was discovered by two men on the side of a road near the small village of Oallen, about 230km (143 miles) south-west of Sydney. On Monday, police announced a murder investigation, sparking intense interest in the case but backtracked hours later, saying forensic testing had proved the contents were not human. The contents in the suitcase were "mistaken for a human originally, so they are very realistic in terms of looking like human remains," said Supt Linda Bradbury from the Hume Police District. "But we've confirmed by other means that they are not." The doll was wearing clothing, had hair and a nose piercing," police said, adding that "the item also had markings that resembled bruises and grazes". Supt Bradbury said forensic teams and investigators had attended the scene on Sunday and that all processes had been followed. "The idea is to not disturb crime scenes as much as possible, to maintain the integrity of our investigation," Bradbury said, adding she had "no regrets" about how the case was handled. Hours earlier, Bradbury had told media that it has been "quite a shocking discovery" for the two men who found the suitcase. "Unfortunately, they were on a weekend drive as a lot of people do over the weekend and stopped for a break," she said. She said the pair had made the "right decision" to report the find. "They were affected yesterday and we will be in touch to let them know that it was not human remains," Bradbury said. Police have now closed their investigations.

item.title: Battle for Mali base has killed dozens of militants, army says
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly8j7ygwvlo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Battle for Mali base has killed dozens of militants, army says - Published The authorities in Mali say their soldiers killed dozens of militant Islamists as they repelled an attack on a military base on Sunday. Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), a jihadist group affiliated to al-Qaeda, said it was behind the assault where its fighters took control of the base in the town of San. The army, which also suffered casualties, disputed it had ceded control - but said its soldiers had to "retreat temporarily". It comes as Mali's security situation appears to be deteriorating, more than a decade after a jihadist insurgency began taking root in the north of the country. "The enemy was eliminated and the attack was successfully repelled. Around 40 terrorists were eliminated," Lt Col El Oumrani, the commander of the 23rd regiment in the San garrison, said in a video. He urged residents to remain vigilant, insisting that his soldiers had "not gone anywhere" and the base remained under army control. "The camp of the 23rd is not empty, it is under the custody of the army." The attack started at around 05:00 local time (GMT) on Sunday and lasted for about two hours, according to witnesses quoted by the French broadcaster RFI. The attackers came on motorcycles and on foot, some disguised in army uniforms to infiltrate the base, RFI reported the witnesses as saying. One said the militants entered the camp and held it "for a long time before leaving". "I noticed that the fighting took place between 200 and 300 metres from the camp. Several terrorists were killed by soldiers, but others fled; some even hid in houses and others went into the forest," the witness said. At least 10 soldiers were killed in the fighting and the assailants briefly took over the camp, the AFP news agency quoted security and local sources. The army told national broadcaster ORTM that the militants used drones, heavy machine guns and armoured vehicles to breach the site's perimeter. Since 2012, Mali has been plagued by insurgencies and large parts of the north and east of the country remain outside government control. April saw nationwide, co-ordinated attacks by an alliance of jihadists and separatist rebels in the north - the Azawad Liberation Front - seeking to overthrow the military regime of Gen Assimi Goïta, who seized power in a coup in 2020. During the attacks, Defence Minister Sadio Camara was killed in an apparent suicide truck bombing on his residence near the capital, Bamako. JNIM has diversified its operations and begun targeting not only northern Mali but also central and southern Mali, showing an ability to penetrate deeper into the territory despite numerous military operations. In the wake of the coup, which was in part carried out over the failure to ease the security situation, Mali rejected French military help and instead turned to Russia. item.title: Israel rejects Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, Netanyahu says
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5yw4lpe0yeo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Israel rejects Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, Netanyahu says - Published Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected US President Donald Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, stating that no military pull-out will happen until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed. Trump's Board of Peace said last month it had reached an agreement for the "complete disarmament" of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza. But Hamas said handing over its heavy weapons was contingent on Israel ending "all forms of aggression" and withdrawing its forces from Gaza. On Sunday, a senior Board of Peace official insisted the US-backed peace plan for the territory remained the only way forward. Israel has continued to carry out strikes on Gaza since agreeing to an initial ceasefire in the territory last October. "Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu said at a cabinet meeting on Sunday. The Israeli military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens", he added. A Hamas official told the BBC on Sunday the group "reaffirms it commitment" to the agreement and it was ready "to engage seriously and responsibly in implementing" the 15-point plan. They called on mediators to ensure "that all parties comply with what has been agreed". Israel's rejection signals another blow for Trump's Gaza peace plan which was announced in September last year. The plan included the creation of the Board of Peace to oversee the agreement's implementation, as well as the disarmament of Hamas, withdrawal of Israeli troops and reconstruction of Gaza. - What's in the Gaza peace deal roadmap? - Published31 July Netanyahu's statement does not come as a surprise. But he has taken some time to make it, perhaps reflecting the difficult position the Israeli leader is in. He clearly is unhappy with Trump's plan but at the same time he will not want to upset his closest ally. It's just over a week since Trump announced what he called a "monumental step toward lasting peace and security" - that Hamas for the first time had agreed to disarm, on condition that Israel withdraws its forces from Gaza. On Sunday, Netanyahu was clear that was not going to happen under his watch. He said Hamas had to disarm first, adding that it couldn't be some "fictitious disarmament" - it had to be real. The reality is any disarmament and withdrawal of Israeli forces would likely need to be phased. Netanyahu said he was now in discussion with US officials about how to go forward. "They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters," he said. But just months before Israeli elections and under pressure from members of his right-wing coalition to take a tough stance on Gaza, he is unlikely to want to make concessions. He has faced calls from far-right parts of the coalition to hold a new cabinet vote and end the Gaza plan, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir who dismissed the draft as "not acceptable". Nickolay Mladenov - a senior diplomat tasked with implementing Donald Trump's peace plan - defended the plan on Sunday and said discussions were ongoing in the hope of a "positive outcome". The board's high representative for Gaza told Israel's Channel 12 that Israel had been asked "to give the process a chance" and said the plan was "the only way forward" to ensure there was no repeat of the 7 October 2023 attack by Hamas. Mladenov said the plan was built on a process that was "verifiable, that is reversible, that at each stage can be stopped, and that we have built up with a very clear-eyed understanding of what are the challenges ahead". He also said that Israel would not be required to withdraw until it could be verified that Hamas was taking steps to disarm. According to the United Nations, about 1.9 million people - 90% of Gaza's population - have been displaced in the territory since the war in Gaza started. The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage. Israel responded to the attack by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations. item.title: Suspected crime boss Kinahan spends first night in custody in Ireland
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62qd5plzp6o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Suspected crime boss Kinahan spends first night in custody in Ireland - Published Suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan, one of the world's most wanted men, has spent his first night in custody in Ireland after being extradited from Dubai. The 49-year-old appeared before Dublin's Special Criminal Court court on Sunday for a 13-minute non-jury hearing, where he was remanded in custody until 5 October. He has been charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation between 18 October 2015 and 6 April 2017. When it was explained to Kinahan that he could file an application for bail through the High Court, he replied: "I think we all know I won't be getting bail, but thank you for your time." An Irish government jet carrying Kinahan landed in Dublin after 18:00 local time. He was arrested and charged upon his arrival. Heavy police operation After his arrival and arrest at Baldonnell Casement Aerodrome on Sunday evening, he was directly transported under heavy police guard to the Criminal Courts of Justice in Dublin. All the benches were full in a packed courtroom of journalists, a number of solicitors from the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP), some members of the public and court clerks. In court, Kinahan was sitting on a wooden bench and wearing a black hooded top. He appeared before judges Patrick McGrath, Sarah Berkeley and Fiona Lydon, and rose to his feet when the three judges took their places. Kinahan did not have legal representation, and told the court that he did not have time to arrange this. When Judge McGrath suggested that he should be charged today and legal representation arranged later on, Kinahan replied: "If I have time, yes." Det Sgt Colm Davison told the court he arrested Kinahan earlier that evening. Judge McGrath asked Kinahan if he would like to appear at the next court sitting in person or via videolink. Kinahan asked if he had to "decide now" and it was explained to him he could make a decision later and notify the governor in the prison. A large-scale security operation was in place ahead of Sunday's hearing. Ahead of the extradition, the Irish Prison Service bought a bulletproof and bombproof van which can be used to escort prisoners who are considered high-risk. Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly said the arrest shows the force's determination to "target transnational organised crime groups" alongside international policing partners such as Dubai police. He added it shows the value of the force's relationship with the authorities in the UAE, the Irish ministry of justice at judicial level, and "on a police-to-police basis". Who is Daniel Kinahan? Kinahan was arrested in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in April. He appealed the extradition order over the past few months but his attempts were unsuccessful. The National Crime Agency (NCA) has previously said that the Kinahan cartel has been responsible for importing tonnes of drugs and firearms around the world and has also been linked to more than a dozen gangland murders. Kinahan was not only wanted by the authorities in Ireland - the US Treasury Department once described the Kinahan cartel as one of the most dangerous in the world. The US government imposed sanctions on Kinahan in April 2022 after identifying him and other members of his family as leaders of the Kinahan organised crime cartel. He fought attempts to extradite him back to his native country, where the Kinahan cartel was involved in a long-running gangland feud that claimed 18 lives. On 5 February 2016, an attempt was made on Kinahan's life in what became known as the Regency Hotel shooting. One of his associates, David Byrne, was shot dead, while two others were shot and injured. This incident was part of what became known as the Hutch-Kinahan feud. Kinahan also had ties to the world of sport via his now defunct boxing management company MTK Global, which represented more than 100 boxers including Tyson Fury and Carl Frampton. 'Landmark of judicial cooperation' The UAE and Ireland have an extradition treaty and on Sunday justice ministers from both jurisdictions issued a joint statement welcoming Kinahan's extradition. "The Irish national is regarded as one of the most high-profile individuals sought for prosecution in connection with transnational organised crime and is accused of directing an organised crime organisation," it stated. Irish Justice Minister Jim O'Callaghan described the extradition as a "landmark of judicial cooperation between the two countries". He also commended "the professionalism, efficiency, and diligence demonstrated by the UAE judicial authorities throughout the extradition proceedings". His UAE counterpart, Abdullah bin Sultan bin Awad Al Nuaimi, said it underscored "the steadfast commitment we have to supporting global efforts to combat transnational organised crime". The extradition agreement was previously used to extradite Sean McGovern, a "senior lieutenant" in the Kinahan organised crime group. He was sentenced to 24 years in prison in June for directing the activities of a criminal organisation. What is the Kinahan cartel? According to former Garda Commissioner Drew Harris, the gang is estimated to have made more than €1bn (£857,870,000) globally from its activities. The US Treasury Department has in the past compared the gang to crime organisations such as Italy's Camorra, Mexico's Los Zetas and Japan's Yakuza. A reward of up to $5m (£3.7m) has also been offered by the US for information on Daniel, his father Christopher Snr and brother Christopher Jnr. In 2022, Thomas Kavanagh, who the NCA said ran the group's criminal operations in the UK, was jailed for 21 years alongside Gary Vickery and Daniel Canning, who were sentenced to 20 years and 19 and a half years respectively. The NCA said evidence showed they were responsible for cocaine imports estimated to be up to £23.4m, and cannabis imports worth about £6.4m. Kinahan himself became a target for murder and escaped an attempt on his life during a fatal shooting at a Dublin hotel in 2016. He left Ireland and spent time living in Spain and more recently in Dubai, where a warrant for his arrest was issued by the Irish courts in April. Daniel Kinahan's lawyer previously told BBC Panorama that he has no criminal record or convictions and allegations about him being a crime boss are false and have no evidential basis.

item.title: Drones spotted over German base days after Leipzig bomb incident
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyeg1ljp2eo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Drones spotted over German base days after Leipzig bomb incident - Published Two drones were spotted over a military base in western Germany just days after an explosive-laden device was found at Leipzig airport. Germany's armed forces (Bundeswehr) confirmed they were seen on Thursday evening at a base in Mechernich, near Bonn, reportedly housing components for US-made Patriot air-defence systems. A spokeswoman for the Bundeswehr Joint Force Command said military police were deployed to the site before the matter was handed over to local police. It is the latest instance of drones being spotted near military bases or airports in European nations supporting Ukraine in its war with Russia, on which suspicion has fallen. Moscow has consistently denied any involvement. German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told newspaper Bild on Sunday that Germany had become a regular target of "destabilising" attacks. "We're not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare," he said. Germany is currently investigating how a drone laden with explosives was able to reach a runway at Leipzig/Halle airport, which is used by Nato, the Germany military and serves as a base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines. The Bundeswehr declined to comment on the ongoing investigation when asked by the BBC on Sunday about the suspected origins of the drones spotted above Mechernich. The local police force has been contacted for comment. German media reports that the base has a storage facility for equipment and spare parts used to maintain the Patriot missile batteries. The air-defence systems have become crucial to Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian ballistic missiles since Moscow's full-scale invasion began in 2022. However, President Volodymyr Zelensky this week pleaded to allies for further supplies, warning that Ukraine was running out of interceptor missiles. After initially offering Ukraine license to make Patriots in early July, US President Donald Trump last week denied any such agreement. A spate of drone sightings in European airspace last year left the continent on high alert, prompting the EU to discuss a continent-wide "drone wall" of air defences. Some European officials have blamed Russia for these drone sightings, claims Moscow has previously described as "absurd". - Published4 days ago - Published3 days ago - Published25 September 2025

item.title: Ancient Roman shipwreck discovered off Sicily coast
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgx1kpz17go?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Ancient Roman shipwreck discovered off Sicily coast - Published Italian divers have discovered an ancient Roman shipwreck off the coast of Sicily, believed to be more than 2,000 years old. The vessel was found piled high with hundreds of well-preserved containers, which were used to transport goods such as wine and olive oil. Italy's Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli hailed the wreck as "one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years". Specialist police divers found the ship around 46m (150ft) deep, after a tip-off from fishermen. The wreckage is 21m (69ft) long and 6m (20ft) wide, according to reports in local media. The culture ministry says it dates from the second or 1st Century BC. Fisherman and free-diver Giacomo De Mola described stumbling across the historic vessel while surveying the seabed near Mazara del Vallo. He wrote on social media that he had decided to dive and investigate after seeing something that appeared to be a large rock on his scanner. "I get closer. And my heart stops. It wasn't a rock," he said. Instead, he saw hundreds of amphorae - tall ceramic jars used to store goods in the ancient era, mostly wine, oil or grain. "This is, without a doubt, the most incredible discovery of my life," he said. "It's hard to describe what it feels like to be among the first humans, in nearly 20 centuries, to see that place again." He posted a video of the wreck, showing eels, snappers and "countless marine life" living among the jars, noting: "The sea never ceases to amaze us. "This time we didn't just find a wreck, we found a piece of our history." Specialist divers from the cultural heritage protection arm of Italy's police, known as the Carabinieri Art Squad, were sent to the site. Officials say safety measures will be taken to safeguard it while it undergoes investigation, as experts work to determine the nature of the wreck and learn more about its cargo. The Mediterranean seabed is thought to be scattered with similar ancient wrecks. Another 1st or 2nd Century BC vessel was found north-west of Rome in 2023, again laden with hundreds of amphorae. In 2018, a Greek merchant ship dating back more than 2,400 years was found lying on its side off the Bulgarian coast. At the time, it was hailed as the world's oldest-known intact shipwreck. item.title: Residents warned to brace for the worst as Canada wildfire rages out of control
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx25dkwk3e3o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Residents warned to brace for the worst as Canada wildfire rages out of control - Published A state of emergency has been declared after thousands of people were forced to flee their homes as a fast-moving wildfire spread rapidly in western Canada, doubling in size since it was first detected on Friday. Police said one person has died in the Bald Range fire, which is burning across 53 sq miles (136 sq km) in Summerland and other areas of British Columbia, according to the BC Wildfire Service. "We have to brace ourselves for the worst," Summerland Mayor Doug Holmes told Reuters. The Summerland area has been forced to evacuate along with thousands of others in nearby communities. Officials said flames were so high they had created their own weather systems, which creates lightning. Canadian police said on Sunday an 80-year-old woman from Meadow Valley, north-west of Summerland, had died suddenly while attempting to flee her home along with a member of her family. "Police believe her death to be a result of the wildfire," police said in a statement. Keegan Radomski who lives in Summerland said she evacuated her home just moments before the fire reached her property. In a video she shared with the BBC, burning tree tops are seen just over the hill beyond the road where Radomski made her escape. "This is right by our house," she said in the video, her voice trembling. Radomski said she has been unable to return since she fled with seven others on Friday. Now they're anxiously waiting on word whether they will still have a home to return to. She said some neighbours who stayed behind have reported many homes on their street burned down. "There are homes that have been confirmed gone, and a lot are in the area near our home. So, we're pretty scared," she said. "The uncertainty is scary." Residents that spoke to the BBC described the wildfire as one that intensified dramatically with little warning before it reached its current size of 13,618 hectares, external (33,650 acres). British Columbia Premier David Eby told a news conference on Saturday that one fire official had likened the fire to "a bomb going off". "Homes have been lost, and properties have been destroyed. Some people became trapped as conditions changed very quickly, and needed to be rescued," the premier said. A state of emergency allows the provincial government access to special powers including travel restrictions and supply protections to prevent price gouging, and extra resources to coordinate rescue work. Summerland, which has a population of about 12,000 people, has been one of the hardest hit areas and forced to evacuate. So were residents in parts of Peachland, which is home to about 6,500 residents. "We have been on evacuation alert many times," said Earl Kurz, a Peachland resident of 30 years. "This is the first time we were actually evacuated." Kurz was on a boat with his wife in Okanagan Lake on Friday afternoon, when he saw clear blue skies rapidly turn hazy grey. By nightfall, dark clouds of smoke above a raging wildfire came into view. It was headed towards Kurz. "We watched it from the lake," he said. "It was unreal." Hours later, police knocked on his door and ordered him and his wife to evacuate. Kurz said they are now safe in a camper miles away. The Bald Range wildfires triggered the largest evacuation event this summer and more than 20,000 people across British Columbia have evacuated their homes, officials say. "A lot of farms have been affected. We don't know how many structures have been lost. They're still busy fighting the fire," Summerland Mayor Doug Holmes said. Hundreds of residents living in Summerland care facilities, including senior housing, were being relocated to safer areas, according to Interior Health, a publicly funded health authority in BC. It was not yet clear how many structures had been destroyed in the blaze. The regional districts of Central Okanagan and Okanagan-Similkameen, as well as Snpink'tn Indian Band and the districts of Summerland and Peachland have issued evacuation orders, with evacuation alerts in some areas, according wildfire officials. In Okanagan, there are a lot of horses that residents have been struggling to evacuate, Canadian broadcaster CBC reported. Those unable to relocate their animals left their gates open in the hope the animals would find their own way to safety, local residents told CBC. Some owners also painted markings on their animals to make them easier to identify later, according to the outlet. Hundreds of wildfires have raged across Canada this summer, with nearly 200 burning in Ontario in July, sending air quality in Toronto to one of the worst levels in the world for a few days. Smoke from those Canadian wildfires drifted down into parts of the US, including Minnesota and New York, leading US President Donald Trump to threaten new tariffs on the US's northern neighbour.
